long_articles.content:
On Monday, Apple announced [record fourth-quarter earnings](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/11/apple-reports-fourth-quarter-results/), with total revenue of $114.5B, up 12 percent from the year-ago quarter. iPhone revenue was up 17.5%, Mac revenue was up 23.7%, and Services revenue was up 9.8%. Wearables revenue was down 7.9% and iPad revenue was down 10.4%.

Apple execs spent an hour on the phone with financial industry analysts. [We’ve got our usual transcript](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/hello-everyone-its-john-apples-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). And I wrote a piece with [my overall thoughts on the results and earnings call](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/he-admit-it-notes-from-another-record-apple-quarter/).

long_articles.title: Prove you are not a child
long_articles.summary:
I'm 100% for banning social media for children. I would even extend it to banning it all together in its current form. But I am also against the methods for enforcement.

        The problem with bann
long_articles.content:
I'm 100% for banning social media for children. I would even extend it to banning it all together in its current form. But I am also against the methods for enforcement.

        The problem with banning social media for one group and not another is that you have to differentiate the different groups somehow. And right now, in an age where information and personal data means everything, there are several entities that are salivating to get this data.

I've written before about all the problems that come from [uploading sensitive data online](https://idiallo.com/blog/your-id-online-and-offline). It doesn't even matter if they delete the data afterward, as long as the data goes through the wire in the first place, there is a chance for a leak.

> What appears to be the same simple request "please verify your identity", becomes fundamentally different when mediated by technology. The question isn't whether these digital systems will be compromised, but when. And unlike that movie theater clerk who can't perfectly recall my birthdate minutes after seeing it, computers have perfect memory. They store, copy, backup, and transmit our most sensitive information through networks we don't control, to companies we've never heard of, under policies we'll never read.

When kids are not allowed to use social media, it's the adult who pays the price. It's the adult who has to prove that they are not children. They have to risk uploading their government ID to a third party, or biometric data that may be saved and backed up forever. 

I reject this method. 

I also reject the method where I have to provide my age to the operating system. No system should compel me to provide personal data in order to use it. Especially if this feature is intended to provide the information to a third party. And what happens if I don't provide this information to my freebsd machine? Or worse, what if I provide false information? Am I going to get punished? How does that protect children in any way?

> Breaking news: Grown up arrested when OS reported forged identity in his laptop.

One question I asked myself was what happens when a minor circumvents the ban. What are the consequences? At least in Australia, a country that has implemented a social media ban for those under 16, [there are no consequences](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/16/australia-social-media-ban-explained-01038852).

> The law places legal responsibility on platforms, not children or parents, and it currently applies to Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.

This almost sounds reasonable. Why should you care, if it becomes facebook responsibility when you don't even own a facebook account? But there is always a caveat. When facebook becomes a tool your school uses to communicate with parents. When Google classroom is the service students use to do their homework. When you are required to login on a system to receive government service. You may not care about a particular social media, but they raise the bar for every other entrant in the game. Every website frequented by a large number of people inherently become social media, and demand data you didn't need to provide before.

Technology is not a magical thing that can just solve every problem. It is especially weak when it comes to social problems. However, society can use technology to solve their problems. The responsibility of children falls onto their parents. And there are great tools for parents that their kids access on their devices.

long_articles.title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
long_articles.summary:
A recent [paper](https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/) argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t.

The paper show
long_articles.content:
A recent [paper](https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/) argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t.

The paper shows that GPT-6 Astra can take a small neural network and interact with its weights directly, “well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms”. Specifically, Astra was able to identify what games a small network[1](#fn-1) was trained to play just by looking at the weights, and even tweak the weights itself. The most impressive result is Astra significantly improving a 0.8B Qwen LLM’s ability on mathematics by natively editing its weights. The reason to be excited here is that “superhuman ability to improve language models” is precisely the kind of thing that could cause recursive self-improvement.

**I think a smart human ML researcher could perform all of these tasks**. Figuring out what game a model was trained to play based on the network sounds impressive until you consider three points:

- The input channels of the model directly listen to each 8x8 grid cell

- The input channels are *labeled* (e.g. “agent”, “moving objects”)

- It’s thus relatively trivial to calculate[2](#fn-2) which parts of the grid the first layer of weights cares about and why

Here’s that calculation expressed as a heatmap in three lines of Python:

```
d = np.load("a9f535cc.npz")
W1 = d["actor/dense1/kernel"]
norms = np.linalg.norm(W1.reshape(10,10,5,32).transpose(2,0,1,3), axis=-1)  # 5 x 10 x 10
```

And here’s the heatmap for each game:

[![fig1](https://seangoedecke.com/llms-are-not-superhuman-at-reading-and-writing-neural-network-weights/J3JiNrBTkY-590.png)](https://seangoedecke.com/llms-are-not-superhuman-at-reading-and-writing-neural-network-weights/fig1_layer1_magnitude.png)

If someone showed you that heatmap without the game labels, I think you’d be able to immediately identify at least the first three games purely by noticing where the player is (e.g. for Breakout, in a horizontal line at the bottom) and where the moving objects are (e.g. for Pac-Man, in the distinctive Pac-Man maze). It’s neat[3](#fn-3) that Astra was able to calculate the norms in its head without executing Python, but not *that* impressive, and certainly not something that should shock anyone who’s been paying attention.

I’m not going to go through each example[4](#fn-4) in the paper, so let’s skip straight to the most impressive one: fixing a 0.8B Qwen model’s ability to do mathematics. 0.8B is a lot of parameters, and “mathematics” is way more complicated than “guess what the game is based on how the player moves”, and editing weights is arguably harder than parsing them. What happened here?

First, note that the Qwen model was not “bad at mathematics” in a pure capabilities sense. It had a specific problem where after 32k tokens it would get stuck in loops, so any mathematical task that needed more than 32k tokens would automatically fail[5](#fn-5). If you had a model that looped like this, how would you update the weights to fix it? Personally, I would try [steering](https://seangoedecke.com/steering-vectors/): I would write some reasoning texts that looped and some reasoning texts that didn’t, calculate the difference between the looping and non-looping residuals, measure how much each weight contributed to that difference, then try manually trimming those top weights. This is basically the [Heretic](https://github.com/p-e-w/heretic) abliteration playbook.

And this is exactly what Astra did! It wrote four pairs of texts, measured[6](#fn-6) the weights that contributed to looping, started cutting them down and testing if it worked, and ended up finding a patch that stopped the Qwen model from looping, thus making it able to work on mathematical problems for more than 32k tokens. Again, **this is exactly what a competent human researcher could have and would have done.**

It’s cool that Astra was able to make direct weight updates. But we shouldn’t think of this like a radically new capability that will change how AI research is done. We should think of this as analogous to the ability of LLMs to emit machine code and tweak compiled binaries: it’s an impressive trick, but the best way to work with binaries is still to write source code and compile it. Likewise, the best way to update the weights of a model is to train it normally. To the extent that intelligent LLMs help with AI research, they will help by improving *training*, not by magically tweaking model weights directly.

long_articles.title: Audience capture
long_articles.summary: Audience capture is the part that scares me the most about writing on the internet. I have the [soul](https://seangoedecke.com/addicted-to-being-useful/) of an engineer[1](#fn-1): when I see a metric
long_articles.content:
Audience capture is the part that scares me the most about writing on the internet. I have the [soul](https://seangoedecke.com/addicted-to-being-useful/) of an engineer[1](#fn-1): when I see a metric like engagement, I want to improve it. I like to make the number go up.

In fact, the whole environment of online writing is tailor-made to help you make engagement numbers go up. It’s trivial to find out how many people are reading my posts, and from what sources. Hundreds of link aggregators all over the internet have algorithms that will help my most engagement-friendly posts get views, and the comments are helpfully sorted by upvotes so I can read the “best”[2](#fn-2) pieces of feedback straight away. Many platforms are set up to financially reward you for engagement, whether that’s by enabling advertisement or by straight up [paying you out](https://help.x.com/en/using-x/original-content-rewards).

Leaning into this environment is a huge mistake. Views and engagement are valuable to me, but not directly. They are proxy metrics for the things I actually care about:

- Having smart, informed people read and consider my ideas

- Getting feedback from readers who have concrete experience with the topics I write about

- Joining interesting public conversations about the state of the industry

- Convincing people to think like me on points I care deeply about

- Building a reputation as a careful thinker and a good writer[3](#fn-3)

It does not benefit me *at all* to have ten thousand people click through to one of my posts, scan the first sentence, then close the tab. It benefits me only a little[4](#fn-4) to have a hundred people read the title of my post on Hacker News, decide not to click through, and leave their comments in the thread. The set of people who do those things — we could call them “clickers”, as opposed to “readers” — does not really overlap with the set of people who will actually read my posts and think about them. And yet in terms of metrics and engagement, they are indistinguishable.

As with any proxy metric, optimizing it too hard can cause it to diverge from the actual value it’s targeting. This leads to the scariest form of [audience capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audience_capture): being captured by an audience you don’t really even want. Suppose I get a lot of views when I write posts about how stupid it is to use microservices[5](#fn-5), because it’s a hot topic. That gives me a reason to write more posts about microservices. The numbers keep climbing. However, I suspect the set of people who read my posts thoroughly — the audience I *actually* care about — don’t really want to read a bunch of the same screeds about that, so they drift away[6](#fn-6). The people clicking don’t care because they’re not reading the posts anyway. So I’m actually failing, not succeeding: I’m replacing my audience of careful thinkers with a fake audience of clickers and sneerers.

This is not just a post about writing on the internet. In 2025, I wrote [*Trying to impress people you don’t respect*](https://seangoedecke.com/impressing-people/) about how succeeding as an engineer involves, well, impressing people who you may not necessarily respect. The core idea here is **knowing what game you’re playing**. Some games are proxy games, like getting views on posts or having great Jira ticket metrics. Some games are real games, like gaining the respect of people who you respect, or doing technical work you can be proud of, or trying to convince people of things that you believe are true.

The difference is in whether *you* care about the goal of the game, not in whether that goal is objectively valuable. If you really want to get [promoted](https://seangoedecke.com/staff-engineer-promotions/), then that’s a real game; if you just want to do solid technical work, getting promoted might be a proxy game that you play in order to get into a position to do that. But even though you don’t really care about it, it’s easy and tempting to win the proxy game at the expense of the real game: for instance, to [crush Jira tickets](https://seangoedecke.com/party-tricks/) because they’re in front of you instead of doing what will actually get you promoted, or to get views on the internet by playing into clickbait.

Making tradeoffs like this is sometimes fine. For instance, you might decide to impress people you don’t like so you can afford to send your kids to a good school. [Selling out](https://seangoedecke.com/selling-out/) a little bit is good and healthy[7](#fn-7). But do it with eyes open! The absolute worst thing you can do is to sell out *by habit*, in situations where it doesn’t even buy you anything you want.

There are [a](https://seangoedecke.com/john-henry-and-the-llm/) [lot](https://seangoedecke.com/point-by-point-considered-harmful/) [of](https://seangoedecke.com/philosophy-and-ai-interpretability/) [posts](https://seangoedecke.com/luddites-and-ai-datacenters/) that I really enjoyed writing that did not get much attention: typically posts where I get a bit more into the philosophy or history, or posts that are dry technical [explainers](https://seangoedecke.com/tags/explainers/). Some of my most popular posts are [laments](https://seangoedecke.com/will-my-job-still-exist/) about a changing industry that are really just popular because they give people an outlet to share their worries too, not because of anything I wrote. I think it’d be a big mistake to lean into writing more posts like that and fewer posts like this. For one, if I want to just optimize for engagement, why write blogs at all? Why not post ragebait and pornography? But the main reason is that I’m writing for the 5% of readers that will read my posts, think about them, talk to other people about the ideas, email me with their comments, and so on.

Raw view counts help expose my writing to more of those people, but they don’t give me much signal on whether I’m appealing to them or not. For that I have to just rely on my taste, or on the thin signal I get back from the readers who do email and message me with thoughtful responses.

long_articles.title: How to install an app on your Commodore 64
long_articles.summary:
It’s time to install an app! But here in 1986, we still call them “programs,” not apps. So, you’ll want to set aside some time to get started installing a program.

Since you have a Commodore 64, ther
long_articles.content:
It’s time to install an app! But here in 1986, we still call them “programs,” not apps. So, you’ll want to set aside some time to get started installing a program.

Since you have a Commodore 64, there are really only two options for getting new programs this month: *COMPUTE!’s Gazette* and *RUN*, and you have to hope that one of those magazines isn’t sold out at the book store. So let’s get going.

## Go To The App Book Store

You will need to ask your mom if you can ride your bike to the mall. The dirt mall is closer, but the magazine stand at the dirt mall doesn’t carry any *computer* magazines, so you’ll need to take a longer ride to the good mall, where the book store actually has computer magazines. It’s a couple of miles to the mall, so usually you would have a friend come with you, but you called their house and nobody picked up, so today it’s a solo trip.

Only one book store carries computer magazines at this mall; the other one only carries magazines about “serious” topics, but they can order back issues of a magazine for you if you want, you just have to wait a few weeks and they’ll call you when it comes in.

The guy at the book store doesn’t know the difference between the different computer magazines, so you can’t ask him if they have the one you want in stock, and he’s probably not going to answer a kid anyway. So you just have to go through all the titles one by one, and hope nobody put a copy of *People* or *Omni* in front of it by accident.

There are no ratings, and no reviews of the programs themselves. The closest thing you get is the magazine’s own reviews of hardware — modems, mostly — and a cover that promises you the issue has the thing you want. This month’s cover has a “Buyer’s Guide To Modems” banner across the top.

![The cover of COMPUTE!’s Gazette, March 1986 (issue 33), with Survivor as the lead feature and a “Buyer’s Guide To Modems” banner across the top](https://anildash.com/images/c64/gazette-1986-03-cover.jpg)

Once you’ve got a copy of *COMPUTE!’s Gazette* and you’re checking out at the store, you can see that it’s three dollars for the magazine (about nine bucks in 2026 money). If you’re lucky enough to have a five dollar bill, you’ll still have two dollars left over after buying the magazine. That means you’ll have enough money to swing by the record store later and grab a 45 of one of the new singles, like Sheila E.’s “[A Love Bizarre](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hU0WhdxpBAs),” written by Prince, or The Bangles’ “[Manic Monday](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SsmVgoXDq2w),” written by Prince, or Prince and the Revolution’s “[Kiss](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H9tEvfIsDyo),” written by Prince.

## Pick Your Program

Now it’s time to race home with the new magazine in hand. You’ll have to wait for everybody to get off of the TV that’s by the computer so you can switch it over to the channel the computer is on and get down to work.

Turn on the switch, and you’re at the blinking blue cursor where it says `READY.` while the screen is still warming up a bit.

When it comes to installing apps programs, it’s all about options, and this month, we’re spoiled: there are *two*! They’re both games: *Survivor*, an arena game where, “if you’re quick of mind, eye, and hand, you might outfox your opponent,” and *Shifter*. Truly, an embarrassment of riches. Since *Survivor* is the one on the cover, we’ll go with that one.

(Two or three programs a month is pretty typical. That’s… the app store.)

## Type It In

Getting this program running is standard stuff — you just read the article on page 36 that describes the game, and then flip to pages 106 and 107 where there’s the code for a short BASIC loader, and then continue on to pages 107 and 108, where there are 345 rows of densely-packed listings consisting of 9 hexadecimal character pairs, all of which have to be typed in perfectly with zero errors or else your entire game will refuse to run.

A quick sample of the early part of your task looks like this:

![The start of the machine language listing for Survivor, from COMPUTE!’s Gazette, March 1986, page 107](https://anildash.com/images/c64/gazette-1986-03-p107-survivor-listing.jpg)

After you’re done typing that page in, you’re about a quarter of the way done, assuming you didn’t make any mistakes.

Wait, what’s that? *Where* are you supposed to be typing these in? Simply type them into the *MLX* program where you… wait, what’s that? You don’t have the *MLX* utility that’s used to type in machine language code for games and programs listed in the magazine?

Oh, don’t worry, you’ll just need to type in the code for *that* program. There’s an article explaining what *MLX* is, which you can read really quickly on page 93, and then you’ll find the code for it on page 94. That one’s only 100 lines of code, so it should be easy enough to type in. And of course, you’ll know if you made any mistakes when typing, thanks to the *Automatic Proofreader*.

Wait, you don’t have the *Automatic Proofreader* program?

Well, no worries. It’s only another 31 lines of BASIC code, which you can find on page 97. (This one you have to type in perfectly on your own; there’s no proofreader for the proofreader.) Once you do that, you’re all set.

![The Automatic Proofreader article and BASIC listing, from COMPUTE!’s Gazette, March 1986, page 97](https://anildash.com/images/c64/gazette-1986-03-p097-proofreader.jpg)

Now, you can just use the program that lets you enter the program to make your program. It should only take about half an hour to type in the code for the *Automatic Proofreader*, and maybe another hour or two for *MLX*. Let’s call it two hours total between them.

After that, *Survivor* is ~30 lines of BASIC plus ~350 lines of hex code, so… maybe six hours? But at least *MLX* will catch any typos as you go.

Once all of this is complete, be sure to save your work to a floppy disk so you don’t have to type it all in again! If all you have is a cassette deck and you’re saving to tape, it’s going to take probably 10–20 minutes of staring at a blank screen when you save, so set aside some time for that.

In total, it should only take you about 8 hours to have Survivor ready to play, plus however long it takes you to get to the mall, buy a magazine, and come back.

## Ready To Play

(Click or tap to get started.)

[This is *Survivor* by Kevin Mykytyn and Mark Tuttle, from *COMPUTE!’s Gazette*, March 1986, running in the [VICE emulator](https://vice-emu.sourceforge.io/). The game loads and runs on its own, which takes a few seconds.]

Controls: the yellow player uses **W/A/S/D** to move and **F** to fire; the cyan player uses the **arrow keys** to move and **Enter** to fire.

## Next Steps

### The Download

Someday, rather than typing all of this in, you might be able to use your 300 baud modem to download already-created versions of these games and tools. You could dial a local BBS, if there’s one nearby. If you’re unlucky, the only one you can reach is a long-distance call, and you’ll be paying by the minute for as long as you’re connected. Or you could look for a local dial-up number for the Quantum Link online service (which will eventually evolve into America Online!).

Transfer times can range from tens of minutes to hours, and of course during those calls, you are tying up what’s usually the sole voice phone line for the household. Anyone picking up a phone handset in the house threatens to knock your connection offline, forcing you to start the whole process all over again.

### Customization

Now that you’ve enjoyed your game of *Survivor*, there are some fun ways to customize your little computer and give it a personal touch.

Just for context, here’s a to-scale comparison of the screen resolution of your Commodore 64 to the dimensions of an iPhone Duo’s unfolded screen.

Commodore 64 screen compared to the iPhone Duo inner display, at the same pixel scale
A 2670 by 1878 pixel rectangle represents the iPhone Duo inner display. In its top-left corner, drawn at true size, is the Commodore 64 screen: 384 by 272 pixels including border, with a 320 by 200 pixel text area. The C64 fits about 48 times into the Duo display. On hover or focus, the C64 shows its READY. prompt and the Duo shows the 180 by 180 pixel App Store icon at the same scale.

READY.

Commodore 64
384 × 272 pixels (320 × 200 content area)

Icon for scale
180 × 180 pixels

iPhone Duo inner display
2670 × 1878 pixels

Hover over (or tap) the comparison to see a C64 prompt and an App Store icon at the same scale.

You can’t change the wallpaper on your Commodore 64, but you *can* easily change the background colors for both the center area of the screen and the border. All you have to do is manually assign the proper numeric color code to the correct memory register corresponding to the values of each of those settings.

Memory address `53281` will set the background color for the primary content area, and a color code of `1` sets a nice readable white background, so it only takes a simple `POKE 53281,1` command at the prompt, and you’re all set. Similarly, `POKE 53280,4` will make the border of the screen a nice bright purple color, and of course there are a full complement of 16 colors to choose from.

Naturally, none of this customization is stored anywhere permanent, and it will all be lost if you turn off your computer or run a program.

## READY.

I hope you’ve enjoyed this brief overview of how to get one game running on your Commodore 64, and perhaps gained a little appreciation for how things have gotten a bit simpler over the years.

Also, I will be entertaining a motion to return to calling our software “programs” instead of apps once more. Perhaps we could use the term to distinguish the software that’s created by humans actually typing things in, as opposed to the kind that’s merely generated by machines?
